analysis.one_liner: Eliminates tariffs on most trade between the United States and Colombia and locks in investor protections.
analysis.headline: The Senate Finance Committee approved this Colombia trade bill without opposition and put it on the Senate calendar within eight days, but the Senate never voted on it; the identical agreement became law that same month through a companion bill the House passed first.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would approve and carry out the free trade agreement the United States and Colombia signed in 2006. It eliminates tariffs on most goods traded between the two countries, extends duty-free treatment for Colombian and Ecuadorian products under the Andean preference program through mid-2013, and lets foreign investors bring arbitration claims against the United States under the agreement's dispute-settlement rules. It cushions a few import-sensitive industries with safeguard petitions and textile enforcement rules, and pays for the tariff cuts partly with new fees on travelers from Canada and Mexico and an accelerated estimated-tax payment for corporations with $1 billion or more in assets.
analysis.who_benefits: American exporters — manufacturers, farmers, ranchers, and food companies — gain duty-free access to Colombia's market under the agreement's tariff schedule. Multinational companies gain enforceable arbitration rights to challenge government actions that affect their investments. Colombian and Ecuadorian exporters keep duty-free access to the U.S. market under the extended Andean preference program. American consumers see little direct change, because U.S. tariffs on Colombian goods were already low.

how_it_helps.text: Approves the U.S.-Colombia Trade Promotion Agreement and authorizes the President to eliminate or modify tariffs on goods under the agreement's schedule.
Extends duty-free or preferential treatment for products of Colombia and Ecuador under the Andean Trade Preference Act through July 31, 2013.
Makes products and services of Colombia eligible for U.S. government procurement contracts.

Gives firms, trade associations, unions, and groups of workers a petition process to get import relief (up to four years, three for textiles) if a surge of Colombian imports injures a domestic industry, and adds extra duties on agricultural goods when imports exceed 140 percent of an agreed quota volume.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury loses tariff revenue on the goods that become duty-free. To offset some of that, travelers arriving from Canada and Mexico lose their exemption from customs user fees, and corporations with at least $1 billion in assets must pay a slightly larger share of their 2016 estimated taxes earlier. Some U.S. producers face new competition from Colombia, cushioned only by temporary safeguards. More broadly, critics of the deal argued that American workers in tradable industries and Colombian workers, who faced the western hemisphere's worst record of violence against labor organizers, bore the risks while the enforceable protections in the agreement went to investors.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal treasury and some import-competing workers

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes the United States to resolve claims against it through investor-state dispute settlement, the arbitration process under the agreement's investment chapter, giving foreign investors a direct channel to challenge government measures.
The bill exempts the new Commerce Department office that services the agreement's dispute panels from the Freedom of Information Act.

The offsets that pay for the tariff cuts include new customs fees on passengers arriving from Canada and Mexico and an accelerated quarterly estimated-tax payment of 0.5 percent for corporations with at least $1 billion in assets.

Safeguard relief is limited — at most four years for most goods and three for textiles, prohibited after ten and five years respectively — and the President must give Colombia new tariff concessions as compensation when relief is imposed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The deal's clearest, most direct beneficiaries are concentrated: exporters who get duty-free access to Colombia and investors who get enforceable arbitration rights, while the enforceable labor and environmental language sits in side agreements rather than the tariff schedule. Consumers gain only modestly, since U.S. tariffs on Colombian goods were already low, and tariff revenue goes down. Import-sensitive industries got real but temporary cushions. Widely reported criticism at the time centered on Colombia's record of violence against trade unionists and the asymmetry between binding investor protections and weaker labor enforcement — an objection an honest supporter of the deal had to acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: The Finance Committee approved it and put it on the Senate's calendar within eight days, but the Senate never took it up for a vote — the House passed its own identical implementing bill, the Senate passed that one instead, and this bill expired when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Baucus introduced the bill on October 3, 2011 on behalf of himself, Senator Hatch, and Senator McConnell, and President Obama submitted the agreement and its statement of administrative action to Congress that same day.

The Senate referred it to the Finance Committee, which ordered it reported favorably without amendment on October 11, 2011, and it was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 189.
The committee filed its written report on September 20, 2012, but no vote on the bill ever occurred in either chamber before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

The underlying policy did not die: the House passed its own implementing bill for the same agreement in October 2011, the Senate passed that bill instead, and the President signed it, putting the U.S.-Colombia agreement into effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Exporters, agribusiness, and multinational investors got the agreement they sought anyway, through a different legislative vehicle, so the failure of this bill changed nothing for them. The only people arguably better off were the handful of members who avoided casting a recorded vote on a contested trade deal.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start — the Democratic Finance chairman introduced it together with the chamber's top two Republicans — while the opposition it drew came mainly from unions and many Democrats rather than from a party bloc.

industries.note: The bill approves the tariff-elimination schedule the agreement negotiated, giving manufacturers, farmers, and ranchers duty-free access to Colombia's market. The gain comes from new market access rather than from charging consumers more, though the tariff revenue it gives up is public money.

The bill locks in the agreement's investment chapter, under which foreign investors can bring binding arbitration claims against governments, including claims against the United States itself. Critics argued this enforceable channel for investors contrasted with weaker, harder-to-enforce labor protections.
The bill extends Andean Trade Preference duty-free access to the U.S. market through July 31, 2013, keeping cheaper Colombian goods on American shelves.

The bill gives the industry yarn-forward rules of origin, customs verification and enforcement powers, a dedicated three-year textile safeguard, and authority to restrict fabrics not commercially available domestically — real protection against Colombian competition, but the protections expire on fixed timelines.

Farm sectors exposed to Colombian competition get extra duties on agricultural goods once imports exceed 140 percent of an agreed quota volume and a four-year import-surge relief process, though both protections are temporary and relief requires compensating Colombia with new tariff concessions.

industries.industry: Corporations with $1 billion or more in assets
industries.note: As a budget offset, required estimated tax payments in the third quarter of 2016 rise by 0.5 percent — a small, one-time acceleration of cash the government collects, not an increase in total tax owed.

industries.industry: Travelers between the U.S. and Canada or Mexico
industries.note: Eliminating their exemption from customs user fees on arriving passengers shifts the cost of funding customs services onto travelers as part of paying for the tariff cuts.
